problemText: As the last Ice Age ended after about 10,000 BCE, people in Southwest Asia who harvested wild grain began saving and replanting the seeds they liked best. Over hundreds of generations those plants changed into forms that depended on human care and produced far more food. What is this process called?
choices: Sedentism
Domestication
Specialization
Urbanization
hints: The question describes people slowly reshaping wild species into tame, human-dependent ones.

problemText: A Neolithic farming village harvests more grain in a season than its families will eat that year and seals the extra in storage jars. Historians treat this stored extra food as the single most important product of early farming. What is it called?
choices: Irrigation
Sedentism
Surplus
Domestication
hints: The term names food produced beyond what the producers need — food that can be stored, traded, taxed, or fought over.

problemText: Foraging bands moved with the seasons, but farming communities that began storing grain increasingly lived in one place all year. Which explanation best accounts for that shift to permanent settlement?
choices: Neither a planted field nor a full granary can travel, so people stayed put to tend and guard them
Domesticated animals could not survive being moved between pastures
Kings ordered villagers to remain near temples so that taxes could be collected
Melting Ice Age glaciers flooded the land and made all seasonal travel impossible
hints: Ask what a family would have to leave behind if it packed up and followed the seasons.

problemText: Excavations at Catalhoyuk, a settlement in what is now Turkey occupied around 7000 BCE, reveal several thousand residents living in mud-brick houses packed wall to wall and farming the surrounding plain — but no palace, no separate temple district, and no written records of any kind. Which conclusion does this evidence best support?
choices: Catalhoyuk was a seasonal camp rather than a year-round settlement
Writing existed there but was recorded only on materials that decayed
Large permanent settlements could form before kings, state religion, and writing appeared
The residents were foragers who had not yet begun to farm
hints: Compare what the site clearly has (size, permanence, farming) with what it clearly lacks, and ask which of those normally comes first.

problemText: In one fertile region around 6000 BCE, foraging bands and farming villages lived side by side. Over the next thousand years the farming villages spread steadily into forager territory until their descendants occupied nearly all of it — even though skeletons from the farming villages show shorter stature, more tooth decay, and more signs of childhood hunger than the foragers' remains. What best explains the farmers' expansion?
choices: The foragers had exhausted every wild plant and animal in the region
Farming fed far more people from the same amount of land, so farming populations grew faster and pushed outward
Farming demanded less daily labor, leaving farmers healthier and better rested than their neighbors
Farmers possessed iron weapons that foraging bands could not match
hints: The skeletal evidence rules out any answer claiming farmers were healthier or more comfortable — so look for an explanation based on numbers rather than well-being.

problemText: A village occupied continuously from about 7000 to 5000 BCE shows a clear change over time. Its earliest graves hold nearly identical simple goods. Graves from its final centuries range from completely empty to ones containing imported stone beads, copper ornaments, and fine pottery. Storage rooms inside the later houses also vary enormously in size, some many times larger than others. Which interpretation is best supported?
choices: A foreign group conquered the village and buried its own elite there
Falling population left more goods available to bury with each remaining person
A new religion arose that permitted only priests to be buried with any goods
Control over stored surplus let some households accumulate wealth, and those differences hardened into lasting ranks
hints: Two separate lines of evidence change together — burial goods and storage-room size. Look for an explanation that ties them to each other.
Ask what a family with a much larger granary could do over generations that a family with a small one could not.

problemText: When historians ask whether an early society counts as a civilization, they check for a standard set of shared features — among them cities, organized government, social classes, public works, and record-keeping. Which of the following also belongs on that standard list?
choices: Job specialization
Universal literacy
Elected representative assemblies
Factory production of goods
hints: Think about what stored surplus pays for: people who work at one trade full time instead of growing their own food.

problemText: A historian publishes a book in 2019 that analyzes Egyptian tax records originally written around 1300 BCE, and reproduces photographs of several of those records inside the book. How should the book itself be classified?
choices: A primary source, because its subject is ancient Egypt
A secondary source, because it was created long afterward to interpret evidence made by others
A primary source, because it contains photographs of genuine ancient documents
Neither, because tax records count as administrative paperwork rather than historical evidence
hints: Sort by origin, not by topic: ask when the thing in your hands was made, and by whom.

problemText: By about 3100 BCE the Mesopotamian city of Uruk held tens of thousands of residents, most of whom were strangers to one another rather than kin or lifelong neighbors. Historians argue that this density itself generated institutions a village never needed, such as courts, markets, and written rules. Why?
choices: Cities contain more farmland per resident, so more property has to be divided among families
Dense populations reduce the need for records, because news travels quickly by word of mouth
Strangers cannot settle exchanges and disputes through personal familiarity, so impersonal rules, officials, and written records become necessary
Large populations automatically produce more religious festivals than small ones do
hints: In a village of forty people, who enforces a promise? Now ask the same question in a city of forty thousand.

problemText: A clay tablet from a Sumerian temple, dated to roughly 2900 BCE, has been paraphrased by scholars as: "Barley issued for one month to forty-two weavers of the temple household; recorded by the scribe Ur-Shara." Which pair of civilization features does this single record most directly demonstrate?
choices: Monumental architecture and a distinctive artistic style
Job specialization and organized record-keeping supported by stored surplus
Elected government and equal treatment of citizens
Long-distance sea trade paid for with standardized coins
hints: List the jobs the tablet proves existed — including the job of the person who wrote it — and ask where the barley they were paid came from.

problemText: Nearly every surviving written record from early Mesopotamia was produced by scribes working for a temple or a palace. What limitation does this place on the history that can be written from those records?
choices: Clay tablets decay quickly, so almost nothing survives from before 2000 BCE
Records written by paid officials cannot be treated as primary sources
The records prove that nothing of importance happened outside temples and palaces
The records reflect the concerns of elite institutions, leaving farmers, laborers, and women thinly documented
hints: Ask who could write, who employed them, and whose business they were paid to record — then ask whose lives that leaves out.

problemText: Two sites are excavated. Settlement X, occupied around 7000 BCE, housed several thousand people in dwellings of nearly uniform size, with no monuments, no records, and burials that look much alike. Settlement Y, occupied around 3000 BCE, housed roughly twenty thousand people and contains a massive temple platform, workshops full of identical mass-produced bowls, tablets recording grain deliveries, and burials ranging from lavish to bare. Which statement best captures what the comparison shows?
choices: Settlement X cannot have been permanent, since permanence requires monumental building
Settlement Y was the less advanced of the two, since sharp inequality is a sign of social breakdown
Settlement Y shows the full cluster of features historians associate with early civilization, while X shows that large permanent settlements could exist before those features developed
The two settlements must have been in contact with each other, since both were unusually large
hints: Run the standard checklist against each site in turn and mark which features are present at each.
The interesting result is not that Y has more boxes ticked — it is what X being large and permanent with almost none of them ticked tells you about the order in which the features arrived.

problemText: Beginning around 3200 BCE, scribes in southern Mesopotamia recorded quantities of grain and livestock by pressing wedge-shaped marks into tablets of wet clay. What is this writing system called?
choices: Hieroglyphics
Cuneiform
Sanskrit
The Phoenician alphabet
hints: The name of the system comes from the wedge shape of the marks pressed into the clay.

problemText: At the heart of Sumerian cities such as Ur and Uruk stood a ziggurat. What was a ziggurat, and what does its central position indicate about those cities?
choices: A fortified granary, showing that grain was the most valuable property in the city
A royal tomb, showing that Sumerian kings expected an elaborate afterlife
A stepped temple platform for the city's patron god, showing that religion stood at the center of civic life
A public courthouse where the laws of Babylon were read aloud to citizens
hints: Each Sumerian city-state had its own patron deity — ask what building that deity would occupy.

problemText: The Greek writer Herodotus called Egypt "the gift of the Nile." Which feature of the Nile best supports that description?
choices: Its flood arrived on a dependable yearly schedule and left behind a fresh layer of fertile silt
It never flooded, so Egyptian farmland was never damaged by rising water
It flowed southward into the Mediterranean, carrying Egyptian trade goods to Europe
Its rapids made it the fastest travel route between Upper and Lower Egypt
hints: The "gift" was agricultural — think about what the river left on the fields once the water went down.

problemText: Mesopotamia sat on a broad, flat plain with no mountains, deserts, or seas closing it off, and its two rivers flooded unpredictably. Egypt sat in a narrow green valley walled by deserts on both sides, with rapids blocking the river to the south and the sea to the north, and its river flooded on a dependable schedule. Which political difference do historians most often connect to this contrast?
choices: Mesopotamia developed writing several centuries later than Egypt did
Mesopotamia remained a patchwork of rival city-states repeatedly conquered from outside, while Egypt held together as one kingdom for most of three thousand years
Egypt required no irrigation at all, while Mesopotamia depended on it completely
Mesopotamia abandoned kingship in favor of assemblies of ordinary citizens
hints: Ask two questions of each region: how easily can an army walk in, and how easily can one central government send orders and collect taxes across the whole territory?

problemText: A provision of the law code that King Hammurabi of Babylon had carved on a public stone pillar around 1754 BCE has been paraphrased as: "If a man knocks out the tooth of a man of his own rank, his own tooth shall be knocked out; if he knocks out the tooth of a commoner, he shall pay one-third of a measure of silver." What does this provision most directly reveal about Babylonian law?
choices: Every resident of Babylon received identical treatment before the law
Disputes were left to families to settle privately, without any role for the state
Penalties were fixed in advance and publicly known, yet varied according to the social rank of those involved
Punishments were decided case by case according to the king's mood on the day
hints: The provision states two different penalties for the same injury. Ask what changes between the two halves of the sentence — the act, or the person injured?

problemText: Archaeologists working beside the Giza pyramids uncovered a workers' settlement containing bakeries, breweries, skeletons showing set and healed broken bones, and tombs where laborers were buried close to the monument they built. A student concludes from this that the Great Pyramid, finished around 2560 BCE, was built by enslaved foreign captives driven on by force. Which response best corrects that conclusion?
choices: The evidence proves the pyramids were raised by unpaid volunteers who received no food or shelter at all
The evidence shows the pyramids were built many centuries later than historians have claimed
The evidence supports the student, since only enslaved workers would ever be buried beside a royal monument

The evidence points instead to a fed, housed, and medically treated Egyptian workforce, including farmers called up while floodwaters covered their fields; large-scale use of foreign captives belongs mainly to Egyptian periods more than a thousand years later
hints: Go item by item through what was actually found and ask what each detail implies about how the workers were treated.
Then check the dates: the period when Egypt held large numbers of foreign captives came long after this pyramid was completed.

problemText: Kings of the Shang dynasty, which ruled along the Huang He (Yellow River) from about 1600 to 1046 BCE, put questions to their ancestors by heating animal bones and turtle shells until they cracked, then carving the question into the surface. These inscribed objects carry the earliest known Chinese writing. What are they called?
choices: Oracle bones
Quipu cords
Cuneiform tablets
The Vedas
hints: The name describes what the king was doing with the bone: seeking a prediction or answer.

problemText: After overthrowing the Shang in 1046 BCE, the Zhou explained their seizure of power with a doctrine known as the Mandate of Heaven. Which statement best describes that doctrine as the Zhou presented it?
choices: Rule is a permanent inheritance that passes within one family forever
Rule belongs to whichever noble family commands the largest army, regardless of conduct
Rule is granted by an assembly of nobles, who may vote to remove a king
Rule is a conditional grant from Heaven that can be withdrawn from an unjust ruler and given to another
hints: The Zhou needed an argument that made their rebellion legitimate rather than treasonous — so the right to rule had to be something a ruler could lose.

problemText: Harappa and Mohenjo-Daro, occupied between roughly 2600 and 1900 BCE, were laid out on street grids, built from bricks of standard size, and served by public wells and covered drains running beneath the streets. Historians most often cite these features as evidence of what?
choices: Deliberate urban planning and shared standards maintained across a wide region
Constant warfare among neighboring cities
The rule of a single divine king whose tomb dominated the city center
The arrival of Indo-Aryan migrants who rebuilt the cities after 1500 BCE
hints: Bricks of matching size in cities hundreds of miles apart do not happen by chance — ask what has to exist for a standard to be set and kept.

problemText: Historians can name Shang kings, date their wars, and describe what worried them, but cannot name a single ruler of the Indus cities, even though both were large Bronze Age river-valley societies. What best explains this difference?
choices: The people of the Indus cities never developed any form of writing
The Indus was a far smaller and simpler society than Shang China
Shang inscriptions can be read because their characters are ancestral to modern Chinese, while the Indus script remains undeciphered, so Indus history must be built from material remains
Mesopotamian scribes visited Shang China and wrote down its dynasty for later generations
hints: The gap is in what historians can read, not in what the two societies achieved — check each option against that distinction.

problemText: A newly founded Chinese dynasty pours resources into flood-control works along the Huang He and into state granaries that release grain during famines. Under the logic of the Mandate of Heaven, why would a ruler treat such projects as urgent to his own political survival?
choices: Heaven's mandate was awarded only to rulers who completed large construction projects
Floods and famines could be read as signs that Heaven was withdrawing its favor, handing rebels a ready-made justification
The mandate obliged rulers to consult their ancestors through oracle bones before making any decision
Once a dynasty had won a war, the mandate was believed to be permanently secured
hints: The doctrine cuts both ways. Ask how people at the time would explain a famine happening under a particular ruler.

problemText: Three findings are placed side by side. Excavation shows the Indus cities being abandoned gradually from about 1900 BCE, with no destruction layers and no mass battle casualties. Geological work shows river systems in the region shifting and drying and the monsoon weakening across those same centuries. Linguistic and archaeological evidence places the main Indo-Aryan movements into northern India after about 1500 BCE. Which conclusion do the three findings together best support?
choices: Indo-Aryan armies stormed the Indus cities and drove the survivors out
Every Indus city was abandoned suddenly, within a single generation
Because the decline had environmental causes, the Indo-Aryan movements into northern India never took place
The decline was largely environmental and began well before the Indo-Aryan movements, which came later as a gradual migration rather than a conquest
hints: Put the three findings in chronological order before judging any of them as a cause.
Note what the excavations did NOT find — the physical traces a conquest would leave behind.
